summary_findings: Marathi is the only one of the three languages with a substantial indigenous star vocabulary, and it is concentrated almost entirely in the cultivators' calendar rather than in named constellations. The learned layer is straightforwardly borrowed — Molesworth's entry for नक्षत्र (1857, p. 454) lists all twenty-seven Sanskrit mansions with only light Marathi phonology (मृग for मृगशीर्ष, आश्लेषा 'or असाळका', पूर्वा/उत्तरा for the Phalgunīs), and Konkani and Gujarati do the same: Maffei glosses 'Star' simply as neketru (1883, p. 455), and the Bombay Gazetteer's Gujarat volumes give the asterisms as Kritika, Rohini, Arudra, Mragshir, Revti, calling them 'star chambers' (Vol. IX Pt I, 1901, pp. 352-353). Underneath that borrowed layer Marathi has a whole parallel system in which asterisms are renamed for what their rains DO to the crop: उंदऱ्या 'the rats' for Viśākhā, उंदऱ्यामांजऱ्या 'rats-and-cats' for Viśākhā-plus-Anurādhā, दडप्या 'the pressers-down' for Svātī, अडवण्या 'the obstructors' for Jyeṣṭhā, कडप्या 'the sheaves' and अंधळ्या 'the blind ones' both for Citrā, बडवण्या 'the mallets' for Mūla, and an elder/younger pair — म्हातारा 'the old fellow' or थोरला कुंवर for Punarvasu against तरणा 'the youngster' or धाकटा कुंवर for Puṣya. Four genuinely non-Sanskrit figures stand out: the Pleiades as विंचू, a SCORPION (Molesworth p. 756, confirmed by Date p. 2824 — the Kṛttikās are not maidens here); Ursa Major as खाटलें / बाजलें, a COT, which Enthoven (1924, p. 64) fills out as four stars forming a cot with a sleeper on it and three thieves creeping up; the pole star as मेढ, a FORKED FARMYARD STAKE, with a whole non-Brahman divinatory sect (मेढेमत) and a caste of village astrologers (मेढेजोशी) named from it; and Hasta (Corvus) reanalysed as हत्ती, an ELEPHANT, a mishearing of हस्त 'hand' that Molesworth explicitly flags and that has propagated into ritual (हस्तागौर, Gaurī seated on an elephant) and into the revenue gazetteers ('the fall of the Hasti Nakshatra or the Elephant Guest-house', Satara 1885, p. 19; 'the elephant showers', Nasik 1883, p. 15). Konkani, on Maffei's evidence, is nearly bare of sky vocabulary — no Pleiades, no Orion, no Great Bear, no pole star in the whole English-Konkani dictionary — but it yields the single best indigenous name in this file: the Milky Way as molbamārog, 'the road that is on the sky', with a second Hindu-Konkani form dudavat, and with Maffei expressly noting that Ākāśagaṅgā is Marathi and Canarese and 'not used in Konk.' That is the exact inverse of Marathi, where every one of Molesworth's eight Milky Way names is a Sanskrit river of heaven and no folk name appears at all — until Enthoven, whose Deccan informants call it Vastupurush (the cosmic man of the building site) and Kavadgantak. Gujarati is the emptiest of the three: no distinct Gujarati star name was verified from any source. The Gujarati dictionaries (Belsare; Mehta & Mehta) give only borrowed forms, and their Gujarati script is unrecoverable from the available scans; the Gujarat gazetteers show cultivators paying close attention to the nakṣatras but under their Sanskrit names, with the omen-lore attached directly to those names instead of generating new ones as it did in Marathi. What was NOT found anywhere: no Marathi, Konkani or Gujarati name for Sirius that is not built on the Sanskrit hunter (लुब्धक, व्याध, and the folk-etymological लोभी 'the greedy one'); no vernacular name for Canopus, for Alcor, or for the Hyades apart from the Sanskrit cart शकट; no morning-star or evening-star name in Molesworth at all; no bier, plough or hen figure for Ursa Major; no tribal star name in Enthoven's Tribes and Castes of Bombay or in the Khandesh gazetteer's long Bhil sections; and no Konkani Milky Way river.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. विंचू, p. 756
entries.quote: विंचू viñcū m (वृश्र्चिक S or بچھو H) A scorpion. 2 The Pleiades. From the fancied resemblance to a scorpion. 3 A common term for the bits of cord which, in stringing a bedstead &c., are attached to the ends of the lines used in the work.
entries.notes: The single most striking non-Sanskrit sky-name in Marathi lexicography: the Pleiades seen as a SCORPION, not as the Kṛttikās. Independently confirmed by Date's Maharashtra Sabdakosa (p. 2824), which glosses sense 2 as 'कृत्तिकानक्षत्र (विंचवाच्या आकारावरून)' — 'the Kṛttikā nakṣatra, from the shape of a scorpion'. Note the homonym trap: विंचू is also the ordinary word for Scorpius/scorpion, so a bare attestation of विंचू in a text is NOT evidence for the Pleiades.

entries.citation: Y. R. Date et al., Maharashtra Sabdakosa (Poona, 1932-38), s.v. विंचू, p. 2824
entries.quote: विंचू viñcū — पु. १ एक अष्टपाद विषारी प्राणी. हा नांगींने दंश करतो. (अप.) विचुः विचु; इचु. २ कृत्तिकानक्षत्र (विंचवाच्या आकारावरून).
entries.notes: Second, independent attestation of the scorpion-figure for the Pleiades, seventy-five years after Molesworth. Retrieved through DSAL's combined Marathi search (marathi_query.py), because the standalone date_query.py endpoint returns empty pages.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. कात्या, p. 154
entries.quote: कात्या kātyā f pl R The pleiades. Commonly कृत्तिका.
entries.notes: Molesworth's mark R means, per his own preface (p. xvi), 'that the city and province of Rajapur and the country southwards are the seat especially of the currency of the word' — i.e. this is a southern-Konkan form, the Marathi of the Ratnagiri coast bordering the Konkani area. Date (p. 677) gives the derivation कृत्तिका > कृत्तिआ > कात्या, so this is a tadbhava of the Sanskrit name rather than an independent formation — hence 'borrowed', but it is a REGIONAL Sanskritic form, not the tatsama कृत्तिका.

entries.usage_note: कात्याचा पाऊस — the rain that falls under the Kṛttikā nakṣatra
entries.citation: Y. R. Date et al., Maharashtra Sabdakosa (Poona, 1932-38), s.v. कात्या, p. 677
entries.quote: कात्या kātyā — स्त्री. (अव.) (राजा.) कृत्तिका नक्षत्र [कृत्तिका -कृत्तिआ-कात्या] ॰चा पाऊस -पु. कृत्तिका नक्षत्राचा पाऊस.
entries.notes: Date marks the word (राजा.) = Rajapur, agreeing with Molesworth's R, and supplies both the etymology and the agricultural derivative कात्याचा पाऊस, 'the Kṛttikā rain'.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. काथ्या, p. 154
entries.quote: काथ्या kāthyā f pl R The pleiades.
entries.notes: Aspirated doublet of कात्या, same Rajapur/southern-Konkan currency; Date p. 678 likewise marks it (राजा.). Homonym warning: काथ्या is also the everyday Marathi word for coir rope (Berntsen p. 23), and Molesworth carries the two as separate headwords on the same page.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. कृत्तिका, p. 179
entries.quote: कृत्तिका kṛttikā f (S) The third of the lunar mansions, Pleiades.
entries.notes: The tatsama, marked (S) by Molesworth. Representative of the borrowed nakṣatra set as a whole — see summary_findings; the remaining twenty-six are not itemised here.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. तिकांडें, p. 378
entries.quote: तिकांडें tikāṇḍēm n तिकांड्या m The three stars composing the belt of Orion, the arrow of Shiva. See लुब्धक.
entries.notes: A Marathi (Prakritic ति-, not Sanskrit त्रि-) formation on कांड 'shaft, arrow-joint'. It answers the Vedic इषुस् त्रिकाण्डा, 'the three-jointed arrow', but the phonology is vernacular, so it is not simply the Sanskrit word in Marathi dress.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. त्रिकांड्या, p. 391
entries.quote: त्रिकांड्या trikāṇḍyā a (त्रि & कांड Arrow.) The belt of Orion as composed of three stars forming the three कांड or arrows of Shiva. See under लुब्धक.
entries.notes: Semi-sanskritised variant of तिकांडें, with the Sanskrit numeral त्रि restored. Molesworth's own etymological bracket makes the composition explicit.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. शर, p. 782
entries.quote: शर śara m S An arrow. 2 The arrow of Shiva, i. e. the three stars composing the belt of Orion. See under लुब्धक. 3 Distance from the Ecliptic, celestial latitude. 4 The versed sine.
entries.notes: Marked S. Included because it is the hinge of the Śiva-hunter myth that Molesworth spells out under लुब्धक, in which the Belt is the arrow, Orion/Mṛga the buck, and Sirius the hunter.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. लुब्धक, p. 721
entries.quote: लुब्धक lubdhaka m S A hunter. 2 Hence (Shiva having transformed himself into a hunter in order to shoot an arrow, viz. the three stars of the belt of Orion, at Brahmá transformed into a buck and pursuing his own daughter metamorphosed into a doe) The hunter, i.e. Sirius or dog-star.
entries.notes: The fullest 19th-century Marathi statement of the Prajāpati-as-buck myth. Note the local twist: it is Śiva, not Rudra as such, who takes the hunter's form.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. लोभी, p. 725
entries.quote: लोभी lōbhī m (Popular form of लुब्धक S) Sirius or the Dog-star.
entries.notes: A folk-etymological reshaping: लुब्धक 'hunter' is pulled onto the everyday Marathi word लोभी 'greedy, covetous'. Molesworth's phrase 'Popular form' is the register signal.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. व्याध, p. 777
entries.quote: व्याध vyādha m S A hunter or huntsman. Hence the star Sirius. See लुब्धक.
entries.notes: Shortened from मृगव्याध. Still current in modern Marathi as व्याध for Sirius / Canis Major.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. खाटलें, p. 202
entries.quote: खाटलें khāṭalēm n (Dim. of खाट) A small bedstead or cot. 2 Charles's wain, the Bear. खाटल्यावर जाणें To commit incest (esp. with the mother).
entries.notes: The cot-figure: the Dipper's bowl is the frame of a string bed and the handle its legs or its trailing cords. This is the classic Indian vernacular alternative to the Seven Sages, and Marathi has it plainly. Contrast the bier-figure reported for other Indian languages: Molesworth's entries for 'bier' (ओकटें, ओखटें, किरडी) contain no astronomical sense at all.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. खाटलें बाजलें, p. 202
entries.quote: खाटलें khāṭalēm, बाजलें bājalēm n A vulgar term for Ursa Major, Charles's wain. 2 A term for the squares or divisions upon (female) garments.
entries.notes: Reduplicated compound of two words for a string bed. Molesworth's 'vulgar' is a register label, not a judgement of obscenity — it marks the word as of the common people as against the learned सप्तऋषि.

entries.citation: Y. R. Date et al., Maharashtra Sabdakosa (Poona, 1932-38), s.v. खाटलें, p. 863
entries.quote: खाटलें khāṭalēm — न. १ लहान बाज; खाट. २ (कुण.) सप्तऋषी (आकाशांतील तारकापुंज, त्यांच्या आकृतीवरून). ३ बैलगाडी. ४ बाडबिछाना. [खाट]
entries.notes: Date confirms Molesworth and adds the reason — 'from their shape' — and a third sense, बैलगाडी 'bullock-cart', which is a second vehicle-figure for the same group and the exact counterpart of English Charles's Wain. Date tags both खाटलें and खाटलेंबाजलें '(कुण.)'; I could not verify the expansion of that abbreviation, as DSAL's front matter for the Maharashtra Sabdakosa is an un-OCRed image PDF. It is most plausibly कुणबी, the cultivator dialect, which would make the register agricultural.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. सप्तऋषि, p. 820
entries.quote: सप्तऋषि saptar̥ṣi m pl (S) The seven saints of the Brahmarshi order, contemporary with each Manu. The names of the several series differ; the names of the saints of the present Manwantara are कश्यप, अत्रि, भरद्वाज, विश्वामित्र, गौतम, जमदग्नि, वशिष्ठ, or, according to other authority, मरीचि, अत्रि, अंगिरस, पुलस्ति or स्त्या, पुलह, क्रतु, वशिष्ठ. These form, in astronomy, the asterism of Ursa major.
entries.notes: The learned name, marked S, standing alongside the folk खाटलें. Both are current; the split is one of register, not of region.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. अरुंधती, p. 43
entries.quote: अरुंधती arundhatī f S A small star in Ursa major, the wife of वशिष्टऋषि.
entries.notes: Marathi keeps the Sanskrit name and the Vasiṣṭha-Arundhatī marriage association. No vernacular name for Alcor surfaced in any of the four Marathi dictionaries searched.

entries.literal_meaning: a forked stake used as a post
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. मेढ, p. 664
entries.quote: मेढ mēḍha f A forked stake. Used as a post. Hence a short post generally whether forked or not. Pr. हातीं लागली चेड आणि धर मांडवाची मेढ. 2 The polar star.
entries.notes: The best vernacular find for the pole star: an ordinary farmyard word — the forked post that holds up a booth — used for Polaris, the peg the sky is pinned to. It answers the Sanskrit मेढी 'threshing-post' as an image of the pole, but मेढ is the live Marathi noun and Molesworth marks it with no S. Corroborated independently by Vaze (1911), p. 464: 'मेढ mēḍha f A forked stake. The polar star.'

entries.usage_note: the name of a non-Brahman astrological sect and of its practitioners (मेढेजोशी)
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. मेढेमत, p. 665
entries.quote: मेढेमत mēḍhēmata n (मेढ Polar star, मत Dogma or sect.) A persuasion or an order or a set of tenets and notions amongst the Shúdra-people. Founded upon certain astrological calculations proceeding upon the North star. Hence मेढेजोशी or डौरीजोशी.
entries.notes: Not a star-name but the strongest evidence that मेढ 'pole star' was a living, socially embedded word: a whole non-Brahman divinatory tradition, and a caste-title of village astrologers, is named from it.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. धुरु, p. 442
entries.quote: धुरु dhuru m An officer employed in the customs. 2 A caste or an individual of it. 3 (Corr. from ध्रुव S) The polar star.
entries.notes: The Marathi tadbhava of ध्रुव. Attested far earlier than Molesworth: Tulpule & Feldhaus, A Dictionary of Old Marathi, p. 358, s.v. धुरु, cite it from 13th-14th-century texts — 'ना ना ते केवळ धुरुमंडळ: प्रकाशरूप तेजाची झळाळ RS. 1920; कां ढळे धुरु । उनमळौ पडे मेरु UH. 1652' — so the vernacular form has roughly seven centuries of continuous use.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. ध्रुव, p. 446
entries.quote: ध्रुव dhruva m (S) The polar star; also the north pole. 2 The twelfth of the twenty-seven astronomical Yog. 3 The introductory stanza of a song.
entries.notes: The tatsama, and the ordinary modern word (Berntsen, Marathi Teaching Materials, p. 74: 'ध्रुव m. 1. the north star. 2. pole.').

entries.citation: Y. R. Date et al., Maharashtra Sabdakosa (Poona, 1932-38), s.v. ध्रुव (compound ॰मत्स्य), p. 1770
entries.quote: ॰मत्स्य -पु. (ज्यो.) लघुऋक्ष किंवा लघुऋक्षांतील दोन मुख्य तार्‍यांपैकीं एक. दुसरा मुख्य तारा ध्रुव होय.
entries.notes: A 20th-century Marathi constellation vocabulary rather than village usage: Date's own supporting quotation is from a teacher-training manual listing ध्रुवमत्स्य beside सप्तर्षि, नरतुरंगम ('man-horse' = Sagittarius) and ययाति as figures to teach children. Register 'vernacular' in the sense of Marathi-formed, but the milieu is the modern classroom, not folk tradition. Date is also internally unsure whether the word names Ursa Minor as a whole or one of its two bright stars.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. अगस्ति, p. 7
entries.quote: अगस्ति agasti m (S) The name of a saint. He is the Regent of the star Canopus. 2 The star Canopus. 3 Applied appellatively to a Glutton or great eater: because the saint अगस्ति swallowed up the ocean.
entries.notes: Purely Sanskritic; no vernacular Marathi name for Canopus turned up in Molesworth, Vaze, Tulpule or Date, even though Canopus is conspicuous from the Deccan in winter.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. आकाशगंगा, p. 61
entries.quote: आकाशगंगा ākāśagaṅgā f (S) आकाशनदी f (S) The Ganges or river of the sky, the galaxy or milky way.
entries.notes: Every Milky Way name in Molesworth is a Sanskrit river-of-heaven compound — आकाशगंगा, आकाशनदी, देवनदी, मंदाकिनी, वियद्गंगा, सुरनदी, स्वर्गंगा, स्वर्नदी — and all are marked S. Not one folk name (no road, no path, no scattered grain) appears in any of the four Marathi dictionaries. This is a clean negative result.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. मंदाकिनी, p. 629
entries.quote: मंदाकिनी mandākinī f S मंदाकिनीओघ m (Poetry) The current or stream of the celestial Ganges. The Galaxy or milky way. Ex. नीळ गगनावरी सुंदर मंदाकिनीवोघ दिसे शुभ्र.
entries.notes: Molesworth's example line — 'on the blue sky the beautiful stream of the Mandākinī shows white' — is from Marathi poetry, marking this as the literary register.

entries.usage_note: names both the asterism and the rain that falls under it
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. अडवण्या, p. 17
entries.quote: अडवण्या aḍavaṇyā f pl (अडविणें) A term for ज्येष्ठानक्षत्र and for the rain which falls under it.
entries.notes: One of a set of Marathi cultivators' names in which a nakṣatra is renamed for what its rains DO to the crop. From अडविणें 'to obstruct'. Molesworth carries a second, homophonous headword अडवण्या 'that obstructs or hinders' immediately after, confirming the derivation.

entries.usage_note: names both the asterism and its rain
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. अंधळ्या, p. 24
entries.quote: अंधळ्या andhaḷyā f pl A term for चित्रा नक्षञ and for the rain which falls under it.
entries.notes: 'नक्षञ' is a typographical error for नक्षत्र in the DSAL transcription of p. 24; the word intended is unambiguous. Compare the separate general term अंधळें नक्षत्र, 'a blind Nakshatra', below — the two are related but not identical.

entries.usage_note: the rain falls when the bājrī sheaves are laid out to dry
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. कडप्या, p. 128
entries.quote: कडप्या kaḍapyā f pl (कडप An untied sheaf, a reap.) A term for the चित्रानक्षत्र and for the rain which falls under it. Because that rain falls when the कडपें of बाजरी are exposed to dry.
entries.notes: A COMPETING folk name for the same asterism as अंधळ्या — Citrā/Spica has at least two cultivators' names in Molesworth's Marathi, keyed to different consequences of the same rain.

entries.usage_note: the hot spell of Caitra, while the sun is in Citrā; medicinal or magical virtues are attributed to it
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. चित्रांचे ऊन, p. 283
entries.quote: चित्रांचे citrāñcē, ऊन ūna n The heat of the asterism चित्रा in the month चैत्र. Wonderful properties are ascribed to it.
entries.notes: Not a name for the star but for its season — the counterpart, on the hot-weather side, of the rain-names अंधळ्या and कडप्या for the same asterism. Molesworth's dry 'Wonderful properties are ascribed to it' is his usual signal for popular belief he does not endorse.

entries.usage_note: so called because this rain flattens the standing crop
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. दडप्या, p. 400
entries.quote: दडप्या daḍapyā f pl (दडपणें) A term for the स्वातीनक्षत्र and for the rain which falls under it. Because this rain presses down the crops.
entries.notes: From दडपणें 'to press down'. Sits in flat contradiction to the learned lore under स्वाती, where the same rain is the auspicious one that makes pearls — a good illustration of how far the cultivators' sky is from the śāstric one.

entries.usage_note: its rain is held to bring out rats, venomous reptiles and poisonous plants
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. उंदऱ्या, p. 95
entries.quote: उंदऱ्या undaṟyā f pl (उंदीर A rat.) A term for the विशाखानक्षत्र and for the rain which falls under it. Because this rain is supposed to produce or to bring abroad rats and venomous reptiles and poisonous plants very plentifully. Ex. उं॰ लागल्या, पडल्या &c. यंदा उं॰ कोरड्या गेल्या.
entries.notes: Molesworth's usage examples — 'the undaryā have set in / have fallen', 'this year the undaryā went dry' — show the word in ordinary weather talk.

entries.usage_note: the first pair of rains breeds vermin, the second destroys it
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. उंदऱ्यामांजऱ्या, p. 95
entries.quote: उंदऱ्यामांजऱ्या undaṟyāmāñjaṟyā f pl (उंदीर Rat, & मांजर Cat.) A term for the two नक्षत्र called विशाखा & अनुराधा, and for the rain which falls under them. Because, whilst the prevalence of the first is supposed to produce rats, reptiles, and noxious plants, that of the second is supposed to destroy or remove them.
entries.notes: A name for a PAIR of consecutive asterisms taken as one weather unit — Viśākhā (ι Librae) and Anurādhā (δ Scorpii). The sanskrit_db_id points at Viśākhā only; the Anurādhā half corresponds to db id 'anuradha'.

entries.usage_note: named from the heaviness of the rain
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. बडवण्या, p. 562
entries.quote: बडवण्या baḍavaṇyā f pl of बडवणी (Beaters, malls.) A term, from its heaviness, for the rain which falls under मूळमहानक्षत्र.
entries.notes: Molesworth glosses the term as belonging primarily to the rain rather than the asterism; the asterism is named मूळमहानक्षत्र, 'the great Mūla asterism'.

entries.usage_note: cultivators' name for the seventh nakṣatra and its rain; paired with तरणा 'the youngster' for Puṣya
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. म्हातारा, p. 673
entries.quote: म्हातारा mhātārā a (महत्तर S) Old, aged, advanced in years. 2 (masc because पाऊस is understood.) The old fellow. A term amongst agriculturists for पुनर्वसु the seventh nakshatra; as तरणा (The lad or youngster) is for पुष्य the eighth. Pr. म्हाताऱ्यानें केलें नांव तरण्यानें वाहविले गांव.
entries.notes: The proverb Molesworth prints — 'the old man made the name, the young man washed the village away' — is a rain proverb: Punarvasu's rain earns the reputation, Puṣya's does the damage. Confirmed by Date, p. 2554: 'पुनर्वसु नक्षत्राबद्दल शेतकरी लोक म्हणतात. तसेंच पुष्य नक्षत्राला तरणा अशी संज्ञा देतात.'

entries.literal_meaning: the elder son / the big boy
entries.usage_note: cultivators' name for the seventh nakṣatra
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. थोरला कुंवर, p. 398
entries.quote: थोरला thōralā, कुंवर kuṃvara m (The great son or boy, the old fellow.) A term amongst agriculturists for the seventh nakshatra or पुनर्वसु. See further under तरणा.
entries.notes: A second folk name for Punarvasu, from the same elder/younger pairing as म्हातारा ~ तरणा but cast as two princes rather than an old man and a youth.

entries.usage_note: तरणा पाऊस, 'the youngster-rain', the rain of the eighth nakṣatra
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. तरणा, p. 368
entries.quote: तरणा taraṇā a (तरूण S) Young, adult, arrived at puberty. 2 Adolescent. 3 or तरणा पाऊस m (The lad, or youngster-rain.) A name amongst agriculturists for पुष्य or the eighth नक्षत्र; as म्हातारा (The old fellow) is for पुनर्वसु the seventh नक्षत्र.
entries.notes: The younger member of the pair. Molesworth's own cross-references between तरणा, म्हातारा, थोरला कुंवर and धाकटा कुंवर show a coherent four-name system covering just two asterisms.

entries.literal_meaning: the younger son / the little boy
entries.usage_note: cultivators' name for the eighth nakṣatra
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. धाकटा कुंवर, p. 437
entries.quote: धाकटा dhākaṭā, कुंवर kuṃvara m (The lad, the youngster.) A name amongst agriculturists for पुष्य the eighth nakshatra, as म्हातारा (the old fellow) is for पुनर्वसु the seventh nakshatra.
entries.notes: Completes the elder/younger prince pair with थोरला कुंवर.

entries.usage_note: हत्तीचें उथाण, the sultriness of the Hasta period; Pr. पडेल हत्ती तर पाडील भिंती, 'if the elephant falls it will bring down walls' — of torrential rain
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. हत्ती, p. 885
entries.quote: हत्ती hattī m (हस्ती S) An elephant. Pr. हत्तीबरोबर बैलाचें वारगोळें. 2 The thirteenth nakshatra or lunar mansion. Note. This asterism is properly named हस्त, being designated by a hand, not by an elephant. It is by popular understanding, howsoever extensive or established, or howsoever inclusive of the erudite or educated, that it is named हत्ती, and that it acquires references and associations as outpouring heavy rain. Pr. पडेल हत्ती तर पाडील भिंती.
entries.notes: A pure case of folk reanalysis, and Molesworth says so in as many words: हस्त means 'hand', but Marathi speakers — learned ones included — hear हत्ती 'elephant', and the whole weather-imagery of the asterism (an elephant's downpour, walls knocked flat) follows from the mishearing. This is the answer to 'what does Marathi call Corvus': not a crow, an elephant. The reanalysis has entered ritual: Molesworth s.v. हस्तागौर (p. 892) describes 'the image or figure of गौरी seated upon an elephant, and worshiped whilst the sun is in हस्तनक्षत्र', and s.v. गजगौरीव्रत (p. 219) the same rite as performed when 'the sun enters the constellation of elephant'.

entries.usage_note: the second fruit crop of the year, ripening under Hasta
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. हत्तीबार, p. 885
entries.quote: हत्तीबार hattībāra m (Elephant-crop.) A term for the fruit-crop which ripens under हस्तनक्षत्र, i. e. the second crop. The two other crops are मृगबार & आंबेबार.
entries.notes: Shows the star-name in load-bearing agricultural use: the farming year's three fruit crops are named मृगबार, हत्तीबार and आंबेबार, two of the three after asterisms.

modern_star.bayer: α, θ, γ, δ, ε Tauri

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. शकट, p. 779
entries.quote: शकट śakaṭa m (S) A cart. 2 The figure of a cart formed by the five stars composing the fourth lunar asterism. 3 fig. A clog, a person or business that hangs on and impedes.
entries.notes: Marked S, so this is the Sanskrit रोहिणीशकट carried over, not a Marathi invention; but Molesworth's 'five stars' makes it a genuine star-figure statement and it is the only Marathi name I found for the Hyades. Molesworth also carries शकटभेद (p. 779), 'Division of the cart-form asterism called रोहिणी by the moon or a planet passing through it' — the classic Rohiṇī-śakaṭa-bheda omen.

entries.usage_note: Pr. मृगाचे अधीं पेरावें आणि बोंबेचे अधीं पळावें — 'sow before Mṛg, run before the shout'; the onset of the monsoon in Maharashtra is dated to this asterism
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. मृग, p. 663
entries.quote: मृग mṛga m (S) A deer, an antelope. 2 The fifth नक्षत्र or lunar mansion: also the rain that falls under it. Pr. मृगाचे अधीं पेरावें आणि बोंबेचे अधीं पळावें.
entries.notes: The name is Sanskrit; the USE is thoroughly vernacular. मृग is the single most important star-word in the Marathi agricultural calendar — the official revenue year मृगसाल and the Deccan फसलीसाल both begin with it (Molesworth, s.v. मृगसाल p. 663 and फसलीसाल p. 550), and Molesworth's derivatives मृगबार, मृगशितळाई and मृगाचा किडा all key crop, weather and insect to it.

entries.usage_note: the damp chill at the break of the monsoon, under the Mṛga rains
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. मृगशितळाई, p. 663
entries.quote: मृगशितळाई mṛgaśitaḷāī, मृगशितळी mṛgaśitaḷī f The dampness and chilliness of weather that prevails at the beginning of the monsoon, during the falling of the rain of the मृगनक्षत्र.
entries.notes: A weather-word built on a star-name — Marathi formation on मृग + शीतळ.

entries.literal_meaning: the fit state of the ground for sowing; hence the sowing season
entries.usage_note: the sowing seasons are named by asterism: मृगाची-हत्तीची-चित्राची-कृत्तिकेची-रोहिणीची वाफ
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. वाफ, p. 748
entries.quote: वाफ vāpha f (वाप S) The fit state of the ground for sowing (see वापसा): also, by meton., the season or fit time for sowing; as मृगाची-हत्तीची-चित्राची-कृत्तिकेची-रोहिणीची वाफ.
entries.notes: Not a star-name but the frame that makes the star-names matter: the Marathi cultivator's sowing calendar is indexed by asterism — the Mṛga, Hasta, Citrā, Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī 'vāphs'. Note that हत्तीची वाफ uses the folk elephant-form of Hasta, not हस्त.

entries.sky_object: the nakṣatras of the late monsoon following Pūrvā
entries.usage_note: वळवाचा पाऊस, the late-monsoon rain that comes from the east
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. वळवा, p. 740
entries.quote: वळवा vaḷavā f pl (वळणें To turn. The wind and rain having turned and begun to come from the east.) A term for those nakshatras of the rainy months which follow पूर्वा. वळवाचा पाऊस The rain which falls under those nakshatras: also, figuratively, a person of whom there is no calculating whither he will turn.
entries.notes: A vernacular label for a BLOCK of asterisms rather than a single one — Molesworth defines it only as 'those which follow पूर्वा', so it cannot be pinned to particular stars. Left with no sanskrit_db_id and no modern star for that reason. Still current in Marathi as वळवाचा पाऊस for pre- and post-monsoon thundershowers.

entries.sky_object: asterisms generally, in a divinatory sense
entries.usage_note: used in divining for lost property
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. अंधळें नक्षत्र, p. 24
entries.quote: अंधळें andhaḷēm, नक्षत्र nakṣatra n A blind Nakshatra. A common term for Nakshatras, during which a thing lost is not found but after great search.
entries.notes: A folk-astrological class rather than a name for particular stars, hence no identification. Related to but distinct from अंधळ्या, the Citrā rain-name above.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. शेंडेनक्षत्र, p. 799
entries.quote: शेंडेनक्षत्र śēṇḍēnakṣatra, शेंड्येंनक्षत्र śēṇḍyēnnakṣatra n (शेंडी & नक्षत्र. A star with a crest or plume.) A comet.
entries.notes: A Marathi compound on शेंडी, the tuft of hair left at tonsure — the comet as a star wearing the Hindu topknot. The Sanskrit धूमकेतु (Molesworth p. 443, marked S) sits beside it. Molesworth also records at शेंडी sense 3 'the tail of a comet'.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. अस्मानतारा, p. 56
entries.quote: अस्मानतारा asmānatārā m (آسمان کا تارا H) A star. 2 A falling star, a meteor. v तुट. 3 A term of praise for a very fine horse, or accomplished rider, writer, singer, musician &c.
entries.notes: A Persian-via-Hindustani loan, āsmān kā tārā, naturalised in Marathi — vernacular in the sense of not Sanskrit, but the source is Indo-Persian, not indigenous. Molesworth prints the Persian original in Arabic script.

entries.usage_note: तारे तुटणें, 'the stars break off', is the Marathi idiom for meteors
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. तारा, p. 377
entries.quote: तारा tārā m S A star. 2 The pupil of the eye. 3 A meteor, a falling star. v तुट. 4 A firework, a kind of rocket.
entries.notes: The Sanskrit word, but Molesworth's idiom तारे तुटणें is Marathi and shows the vernacular conception of a meteor as a star snapping loose.

entries.usage_note: the word is the ordinary one in weather and night-sky talk; Molesworth records under it a belief in a malign 'blast from the stars'
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. चांदणी, p. 277
entries.quote: चांदणी cāndaṇī f A star. 2 An awning. 3 An ornament (like राखडी, but smaller) for the head of women. 4 A blast from the stars. Supposed to fall on horses if they are uncovered (i. e. without the Jhúl, or some rag or clout) whilst eating their grain. v पड, मार, हाण. 5 An inauspicious mark of the horse,—a white spot on the forehead.
entries.notes: The everyday Marathi word for a star, formed on चंद्र 'moon' and unmarked by Molesworth, i.e. not treated as a Sanskrit loan; तारा and नक्षत्र are both marked S. Sense 4 records a genuine piece of Deccan folk belief — a malign 'blast from the stars' that strikes uncovered horses at their feed. The same entry ends with the proverb चांदण्यांत निजती आणि माडीची हवा पाहती, of one who sleeps under the stars but looks for the breeze of an upper storey.

entries.usage_note: नक्षत्रासारखा, 'brilliant as a constellation'; नक्षत्र पडणें (हातावर) 'to have itching hands, be given to thieving'
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. नक्षत्र, p. 454
entries.quote: नक्षत्र nakṣatra n (S) A star. 2 An asterism in the moon's path; a lunar mansion. Twenty-seven are enumerated; viz. अश्विनी, भरणी, कृत्तिका, रोहिणी, मृग or मृगशीर्ष, आर्द्रा, पुनर्वसु, पुष्य, आश्लेषा (or असाळका), मघा, पूर्वा, उत्तरा, हस्त, चित्रा, स्वाती, विशाखा, अनुराधा, ज्येष्ठा, मूल, पूर्वाषाढा, उत्तराषाढा, श्रवण, धनिष्ठा, शततारका, पूर्वाभाद्रपदा, उत्तराभाद्रपदा, रेवती, अभिजित्.
entries.notes: This is the entry that settles the framing question for Marathi: the standard twenty-seven are taken over wholesale from Sanskrit, with only light Marathi phonology (आश्लेषा 'or असाळका', पूर्वा/उत्तरा for the Phalgunīs, मृग for मृगशीर्ष). The interesting Marathi material is not here but in the cultivators' renamings recorded above.

entries.sky_object: Jupiter (mistaken for Venus as morning star)
entries.usage_note: a caravan name: travellers who start their cattle on the false dawn Jupiter announces
entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. बैलमाऱ्या, p. 592
entries.quote: बैलमाऱ्या bailamāṟyā m (Bullock-killer.) A name amongst the वाणी & कुणबी classes for the planet Jupiter. (Because the rising of this planet being sometimes mistaken for that of Venus, and the dawn thus being judged to be approaching, travelers start off their cattle to encounter, it may be, long darkness with all its troubles and accidents).
entries.notes: A planet, not a star, but the best single specimen of Deccan folk sky-knowledge in Molesworth: attributed to named communities (Vāṇī traders and Kuṇbī cultivators), grounded in a practical error — confusing Jupiter's heliacal rising with Venus as morning star — and named for its cost in dead bullocks.

entries.citation: J. T. Molesworth, A Dictionary, Marathi and English, 2nd ed. rev. and enl. (Bombay: Bombay Education Society's Press, 1857), s.v. चटकचांदणें, p. 268
entries.quote: चटकचांदणें caṭakacāndaṇēm n Bright moon-shine. 2 Applied often to the shining of Venus.
entries.notes: The nearest Marathi comes to a distinct name for Venus as an object of ordinary observation. Note what is NOT in Molesworth: no morning-star or evening-star name at all. A full-text search of the dictionary for 'morning star' and 'evening star' returns nothing; Venus appears only as the planet शुक्र (p. 795), its corrupt form सूक (p. 865, 'Corr. of शुक्र S'), and the technical rising/setting vocabulary पूर्वोदय, पश्चिमास्त etc.

entries.usage_note: the four bowl-stars are a cot with a man asleep on it; the three handle-stars are thieves
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 64
entries.quote: The seven stars of the Great Bear are sometimes known as Khatale and Bagale. Four are thought to be a cot with a man asleep thereon, and the other three are thieves.
entries.notes: The fullest telling of the cot-figure I found anywhere: not just a bed, but an occupied bed with three thieves creeping up on it. These are the same two words Molesworth records as खाटलें and बाजलें (1857, p. 202), but Enthoven prints them in roman only, in italic and WITHOUT diacritics — no Devanagari appears anywhere in the book — so name_native is left null here rather than back-supplied from Molesworth. Enthoven gives no community and no district for this name; the book is compiled from questionnaire returns and attributions in its sky chapter are regional at best.

entries.usage_note: reaches the zenith at midnight on a fixed day, which is how the lunar months are named
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 64
entries.quote: The constellation of Mrig consists of seven stars, four like the legs of a cot and three others under them in a line.
entries.notes: IMPORTANT CAUTION for anyone reading cot-figures across Indian languages: on this one page Enthoven applies the cot image to TWO different groups — Orion here, and the Great Bear eight lines later. A bare report that 'the cot' is a folk constellation therefore does not identify a star group by itself. The seven stars of Mrig here are evidently the Belt plus the four corner stars of Orion (Betelgeuse, Bellatrix, Saiph, Rigel), which is not the classical Mṛgaśīrṣa (the three faint stars of the deer's head, λ φ¹ φ² Orionis) — the folk figure has absorbed the whole of Orion.

entries.sky_object: Rohiṇī and Kṛttikā taken together — Aldebaran/Hyades with the Pleiades
entries.usage_note: used to predict the rise and fall of the cotton market
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 68
entries.quote: The Rohini and Krittika constellations, popularly known as Gadli, are supposed to indicate the rise and fall in the cotton-market.
entries.notes: A single folk name covering two adjacent asterisms — Aldebaran with the Hyades, and the Pleiades — i.e. roughly the head of Taurus. Confidence 'likely' rather than 'certain' because Enthoven names the pair but does not say where the group's boundaries fall, and gives no etymology; I could not establish the meaning of Gadli from any dictionary consulted (it is not in Molesworth, Vaze, Tulpule or Date under गडली, गाडली or गादली). Roman only, no script printed. The cotton-market use points to Gujarat or Khandesh, but Enthoven does not say so and I have not assumed it.

entries.literal_meaning: the Vāstu-puruṣa, the cosmic man of the building site
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 72
entries.quote: The Milky Way is known as the Akashganga, Vastupurush, and Kavadgantak.
entries.notes: This corrects what the Marathi dictionaries alone would suggest. Molesworth, Vaze, Tulpule and Date give ONLY Sanskrit river-of-heaven compounds for the Milky Way; Enthoven's ethnography turns up two names that are not rivers at all. Vastupurush is the recumbent cosmic man pegged out under a building plot in Indian architectural ritual — the galaxy read as that figure stretched across the sky.

entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 72
entries.quote: The Milky Way is known as the Akashganga, Vastupurush, and Kavadgantak.
entries.notes: SPELLING CONFLICT within the source: the body text on p. 72 prints Kavadgantak; the book's own index (p. 361) prints Kavadghantak. Both forms are Enthoven's. The first element is very likely कावड kāvaḍ, the shoulder-yoke with a water-pot hung at each end — which would make the Milky Way a carrying-pole across the sky, a figure that would be independent of the Gaṅgā tradition — but Enthoven gives no gloss and I have not found the word in a dictionary, so the etymology is my conjecture and is flagged as such. Confidence 'likely' refers to the name's form, not to the identification of the object, which is explicit.

entries.usage_note: a heliacal-rising marker: every Brahman must worship it within seven days of its first appearance, on pain of seven months' pollution
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 67
entries.quote: Every Brahman must offer arghyas to, and worship, the Agastya constellation, in a hut of Darbha (Eragrostis cynosuroides) and Kasada (Cassia occidentalis) within seven days from the date of its appearance.
entries.notes: The name is Sanskrit but the practice is the point: Canopus is used as a seasonal marker, its heliacal rising in the Deccan falling in late August or early September and closing the first half of the monsoon. The archive.org OCR renders the name 'Agasiya'; the printed page reads Agastya.

entries.usage_note: Konkan death-divination: a person who cannot make out the pole star will die within six months, and some substitute Arundhatī for the pole star
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 68
entries.quote: On the authority of the Mahakala Nirvan Tantra, some people in the Konkan believe that a person who cannot get a view of the pole-star will die within six months ; while others substitute the Arundhati star for the pole-star and determine the duration of life of a diseased person by the same process.
entries.notes: The scan splits 'Tantra' as 'T antra'; the quote gives the printed reading. A Konkan-attributed use, and the only place in this whole compilation where a specific region is attached to a star belief in Enthoven. Compare, on the same page, the parallel omen taken from 'the dimmest star of the Great Bear group' — which is Alcor again, under a description rather than a name.

entries.usage_note: thunder in Rohiṇī portends a Boterun — seventy-two days without rain; lightning from a clear sky in the same asterism causes Rohini-tap, 'the burning heat of Rohiṇī'
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 78
entries.quote: Thunder during the Rohini nakshatra is a bad omen : it foreshadows either a famine, or a Boterun, i. e. complete cessation of rains for seventy-two days, after the thunder-claps are heard.
entries.notes: Boterun and Rohini-tap are both vernacular formations built on the asterism name; Rohini-tap is Rohiṇī + ताप 'burning heat'. The archive.org OCR mangles both words (it prints 'seventy-t wo' and 'Rohini-t^azf' where the italic type sits); the readings given here follow the printed page. On the same page Enthoven adds the counterpart for Hasta: 'Thunder or lightning in the Hasta nakshatra foretells good harvests and a prosperous year.'

entries.usage_note: names the heavy westerly downpour of September, distinguished by cultivators from the regular south-west monsoon
entries.citation: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. XIX: Satara (Bombay: Government Central Press, 1885), p. 19
entries.quote: it is known as the fall of the Hasti Nakshatra or the Elephant Guest-house.
entries.notes: Independent confirmation, from revenue-survey fieldwork rather than a dictionary, of the elephant reading of Hasta that Molesworth records s.v. हत्ती. The sentence quoted is preceded by: 'A heavy burst, often six inches, of westerly rain nearly always happens in September. The people do not regard this as part of the regular south-west monsoon' — that lead-in is quoted here in the printed reading rather than the scan's, which garbles it as 'A heavy bursty often six inches^ of westerly rain nearly alw^ays happens'. The Nasik volume (Vol. XVI, 1883, p. 15) has the same: the rains end 'until the Hasta Nakshatra or sign of the Elephant in the first half of October' (the scan prints 'Rasta'), and it calls the September-October rains 'the elephant showers'. Roman only; no Devanagari is printed in the Gazetteer.

entries.usage_note: worshipped as seven cocoanuts by elderly women, married and widowed, on Ṛṣipañcamī, the bright fifth of Bhādrapada
entries.citation: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. XXII: Dharwar (Bombay: Government Central Press, 1884), p. 71
entries.quote: On this day elderly women, whether married or widows, worship seven cocoanuts, calling them the seven seers Agasti, Angirasa, Atri, Bhrigu, Kashyap, Vasishth, and Vishvamitra, the seven chief stars in the Great Bear which have power to cleanse from sin.
entries.notes: The archive.org scan garbles two words of the quoted sentence — it prints 'muarricd' for 'married' and 'Vishvdmitra' for 'Vishvámitra'; the readings given are the printed ones. Confidence 'disputed' because of the LIST, not the identification of the group. This roster of seven ṛṣis for the Big Dipper — Agasti, Aṅgirasa, Atri, Bhṛgu, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra — matches neither of the two lists Molesworth gives s.v. सप्तऋषि (p. 820), and it puts AGASTI, who is normally Canopus in the far south, among the seven northern stars. Local ritual practice has evidently reshuffled the sages; no per-star mapping can be recovered from it.

entries.usage_note: rain in mṛg is believed to breed insects; rain in punarvasu to breed a stalk-borer in the millets
entries.citation: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. IV: Ahmedabad (Bombay: Government Central Press, 1879), p. 61
entries.quote: With reference to this, as in all the ordinary affairs of life, the cultivators pay great attention to the nakshatras, or twenty-seven lunar mansions of the Hindu zodiac.
entries.notes: The clearest statement that Gujarati cultivators use the Sanskrit twenty-seven, unrenamed. The passage continues (OCR damaged, reading from context): rain during 'the mrig nakshatra which commences on the 5th June' preludes an abundance of insects, and rain in 'the punarvasu nakshatra which commences fourteen or fifteen days afterwards' brings a tiny animal generated inside the millet stalk. Compare the Marathi position, where exactly this cultivators' weather-lore produced a parallel set of NEW names (उंदऱ्या, अडवण्या, म्हातारा …). Gujarat, on this evidence, kept the Sanskrit names and attached the lore to them directly.

entries.usage_note: each asterism carries a dated window and a rain omen: e.g. only a drizzle while the moon is in Kṛttikā (8-21 May) means partial failure of the rains
entries.citation: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. IX Part I: Gujarát Population, Hindus (Bombay: Government Central Press, 1901), pp. 352-353
entries.quote: The year will be one of partial failure of rain if there is only a drizzle during the time the moon remains in the Kritika star chamber.
entries.notes: The Gujarati shapes of the asterism names as the Gazetteer romanises them — Kritika, Rohini, Arudra, Mragshir, Revti — with the Gazetteer's own rendering of nakṣatra as 'star chamber'. Every one is the Sanskrit name in Gujarati phonology; not a single independent Gujarati star-name appears in this chapter or in the volume's separate 'Stars' section (pp. 405-406), which treats stars generically as divine beings, records saying 'Shiv Shiv' at the sight of a meteor, and the showing of the pole star to a newly married couple. Roman only; no Gujarati script is printed anywhere in the Gazetteer.

entries.literal_meaning: the road that is on the sky
entries.citation: A. F. X. Maffei, An English-Konkani Dictionary (Mangalore: Basel Mission Press, 1883), s.v. Galaxy, pp. 201-202
entries.quote: Galaxy, s. molbamarog, -rga, m. =l. the road (which is) on the sky
entries.notes: The best indigenous find in the whole Konkani/Gujarati side of this compilation: the Milky Way as a ROAD, with Maffei supplying his own literal gloss ('=l.' is his abbreviation for 'literal, i.e. translation'). Built on molab 'sky, firmament' (Maffei p. 184, s.v. Firmament: 'molab, -lba, n.; antral, -la, n.; akas, -sa, n.') + mārog 'road'. This is exactly what the Marathi dictionaries do NOT have — Molesworth's eight Milky Way names are all Sanskrit rivers of heaven. Maffei prints roman only in the English-Konkani half (the Konkani-English half uses Kannada script), so no Devanagari is supplied here. The Google scan prints Maffei's abbreviation '=l.' (his mark for 'literal, i.e. translation') as '=1.' and drops the running head into the middle of the entry, which runs across a page break; and the same entry adds two further forms — see the sibling entries for dudavat and for Maffei's explicit denial of Akāsagaṅgā.

entries.usage_note: marked (H. K.) — Maffei's abbreviation for a word used especially by Hindu Konkans, as against the Christian Konkani of Mangalore
entries.citation: A. F. X. Maffei, An English-Konkani Dictionary (Mangalore: Basel Mission Press, 1883), s.v. Galaxy, p. 202
entries.quote: dudavat, -te, f. (H. K.)
entries.notes: A second, community-specific Konkani name for the Milky Way, given in the same entry as molbamārog. Maffei supplies no gloss; the reading 'milk-road' is my conjecture from dudh + vāṭ and is flagged as such — it would be an independent calque on the same idea as Latin via lactea rather than a borrowing from it. Confidence 'likely' covers both the OCR of the form (the scan renders the H.K. mark as '{B. K.}') and the etymology; the identification of the object is explicit and certain. The Konkani-English half of the volume carries what appears to be the same word under a Kannada-script headword glossed 'Galaxy, milky way', marked n.u. = not used.

entries.usage_note: Maffei marks it Mr. Cn. — Marathi and Canarese — and says it is not used in Konkani
entries.citation: A. F. X. Maffei, An English-Konkani Dictionary (Mangalore: Basel Mission Press, 1883), s.v. Galaxy, p. 202
entries.quote: Mr. Cn., but not used in Konk.
entries.notes: A NEGATIVE attestation, and the reason it is worth an entry: Maffei lists the pan-Indian Sanskrit name Ākāśagaṅgā only to rule it out of Konkani, tagging it as Marathi and Canarese. Konkani, on his evidence, calls the Milky Way a road and not a river — the opposite of the Marathi position. The form of the headword itself is badly OCR'd in the Google scan, which prints it as 'Eikagag&tiga' and the following words as 'bui nol used in Konk.'; the roman spelling of the headword given here is the standard one and not a transcription, and the quote gives the printed reading of Maffei's note. Marathi's Ākāśagaṅgā is db id 'akashaganga'.

entries.citation: A. F. X. Maffei, An English-Konkani Dictionary (Mangalore: Basel Mission Press, 1883), s.v. Star, p. 455
entries.quote: Star, s, neketru, -ra, «., pr. fg.
entries.notes: Sanskrit nakṣatra in Konkani phonology, the ordinary word for a star. The '«' is an OCR artefact for 'n.' (neuter); 'pr. fg.' is Maffei's mark for a word used both properly and figuratively. Maffei's entry for Constellation (p. 85) is built on the same stem: 'Constellation, s. neketra[ñ]chi ras' — nakṣatra + rāśi — where the scan garbles the genitive plural.

entries.usage_note: marked (H. K.), i.e. a Hindu Konkani word
entries.citation: A. F. X. Maffei, An English-Konkani Dictionary (Mangalore: Basel Mission Press, 1883), s.v. Comet, p. 73
entries.quote: Comet, s. dumaket, -ta, n.
entries.notes: Sanskrit dhūmaketu in Konkani phonology. Maffei's (H. K.) tag — rendered '{U, K.}' by the scan — is his mark for vocabulary belonging to Hindu rather than Christian Konkani speakers, and it recurs on the Milky Way name dudavat and on Planet (p. 344, 'graha'). Konkani here simply has no separate Christian-register word, which is itself informative about how thin the sky vocabulary of this dictionary is.

caveats: Marathi is over-represented here, and that is a finding rather than a sampling error: Molesworth's 1857 dictionary is by a wide margin the richest source in the set, and DSAL's combined Marathi search puts three further dictionaries (Date's Maharashtra Sabdakosa, Vaze, Tulpule & Feldhaus) behind the same query. Konkani and Gujarati have nothing comparable, so the imbalance in the file partly reflects the imbalance in the lexicography.

SCRIPT DISCIPLINE. name_native is filled only where the source actually prints an Indic script. That is true of every Marathi entry (Molesworth, Vaze, Tulpule and Date all print Devanagari) and of none of the others. Enthoven's Folklore of Bombay prints roman only, in italic and without any diacritics; the Bombay Gazetteer prints roman with acute accents; Maffei's English-Konkani half prints roman only (his Konkani-English half uses Kannada script). Khatale and Bagale are certainly Molesworth's खाटलें and बाजलें, but the Enthoven entries leave name_native null rather than back-supply a script Enthoven never used.

OCR. All the non-DSAL sources were read from archive.org djvu.txt derived from 19th- and early-20th-century scans, and the OCR is damaged. Quotes were taken only from passages that render cleanly, and where a word is known to be mis-scanned this is stated in the entry's notes (Enthoven's Agastya prints as 'Agasiya' and Saptarishi as 'Saftarishi'; Maffei's (H. K.) mark prints variously as '{U, K.}' and '{B. K.}'; the Nasik gazetteer's Hasta prints as 'Rasta'). Where a whole passage was too corrupt to quote, it was left out.

GUJARATI IS THE WEAK POINT, AND THE REASON IS MECHANICAL, NOT SUBSTANTIVE. DSAL has no Gujarati dictionary. Four Gujarati dictionaries on archive.org were downloaded and searched — Belsare's Etymological Gujarati-English Dictionary, both volumes of Mehta & Mehta's Modern Gujarati-English Dictionary, and Montgomery's A Dictionary English and Gujarati (1877) — and their ENGLISH sides confirm that the entries exist and that the expected Sanskritic set is there (Kṛttikā = the Pleiades, Svātī = Arcturus, Saptarṣi = Ursa Major, Dhruva = the polar star, Ākāśagaṅgā = the Milky Way; Montgomery has headwords for both PLEIADES and MILKY-WAY). But in every one of them the Gujarati script and the roman transliterations alike come out of the scan as noise — Montgomery's Gujarati for PLEIADES reads 's(uiSt (t4A)n.' — so no name could be transcribed to the standard this file uses, and none was guessed. The two Gujarati entries here therefore rest on the gazetteers, which romanize. A Gujarati pass with usable page images, or with Shapurji Edalji's 1868 dictionary, is the obvious next step, and it should be aimed squarely at whether Gujarati has anything answering to Marathi's विंचू, खाटलें, मेढ and हत्ती.

THE COT FIGURE IS NOT DIAGNOSTIC. Enthoven applies it, on one page, to both Orion and the Great Bear. A folk report that 'the cot' is a constellation therefore does not by itself identify a star group, and cot-names collected in other Indian languages should not be assumed to mean Ursa Major.

HOMONYM TRAPS. विंचू is the ordinary Marathi word for a scorpion and for Scorpius, so an isolated occurrence is not evidence for the Pleiades. हत्ती is the ordinary word for an elephant. मेढ is the ordinary word for a forked post. काथ्या is also coir rope. खाटलें is also, in Date, a bullock-cart. Every one of these needs its astronomical sense certified by the dictionary, not inferred from context.

COMPETING NAMES, recorded rather than resolved: Citrā (Spica) has two Marathi rain-names, अंधळ्या and कडप्या, keyed to different effects of the same rain; the Milky Way has three names in Enthoven and eight in Molesworth; Punarvasu and Puṣya each have two agriculturists' names; and Enthoven's own index disagrees with his body text on whether the Milky Way name is Kavadgantak or Kavadghantak.

REGIONAL MARKS. Molesworth's R (used on कात्या, काथ्या) means, by his own Preface (p. xvi), the Rajapur district and the country south of it — the southern Konkan, bordering Konkani territory; C means the Konkan generally. Date's mark (कुण.) on खाटलें could not be expanded: DSAL's front matter for the Maharashtra Sabdakosa is an un-OCRed image PDF. It is most plausibly कुणबी, the cultivator dialect, but that is not verified.

DSAL ENDPOINT NOTE for anyone rebuilding this: molesworth_query.py, vaze_query.py and tulpule_query.py support full-text search (matchtype=containing without searchhws), which is how the English-side hunt was done. date_query.py returns empty pages for every query; Date's entries are reachable only through the combined marathi_query.py endpoint, and only by exact headword. Full-text search on marathi_query.py also fails.

OUT OF SCOPE but noted in passing: the Dharwar gazetteer (1884, p. 271) records a distinct Kannada set of 'star-chambers' — Mrigshirshe, A'rdi, Maghe, Hubbe, Hastu, Chette, Dhanishte — grouped into mungári and hingári seasons. The Gujarat Parsi section of the gazetteer (Vol. IX Pt II) gives Avestan star names (Teshtar = Sirius, Haptoiringa = the Great Bear); those belong to Zoroastrian tradition, not to the Gujarati language, and are excluded.
